summary: The reader is built to feel the sadness of things: longing, pity for the women, aesthetic delight in poems and seasons, and unease at desire's costs.

need-to-breathe.why: Nothing is built to affect the reader's breath.

hungry.why: Food is almost absent; nothing makes the reader hungry.

full.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

thirsty.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

gassy.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

need-to-poop.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

need-to-pee.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

sleepy.why: The tale's slow pace is for reverie, not sleep; it does not aim to lull.

nauseous.why: Nothing is built to sicken the reader.

urge-to-sneeze.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

urge-to-cough.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

dizzy.why: Nothing is built to produce vertigo.

fatigued.why: The reader is not made to feel bodily exertion.

pain.why: Illness and death are told with restraint; the reader is not made to wince.

disgusted.why: Suetsumuhana's red nose and the aged Naishi's advances are built for a shudder of comic distaste.

itchy.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

tickled.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

over-stimulated.why: Nothing is built to overwhelm the reader's senses.

too-hot-too-cold.why: Snow and the Suma storm are atmosphere, not built to chill the reader.

afraid.why: Yūgao's death in the dark villa and Rokujō's possessing spirit are built as uncanny terror, the tale's few moments of fear.

anxious.why: The reader is made to dread discovery of Fujitsubo's secret and of Kashiwagi's affair, and to fear for Ukifune.

panic.why: Nothing is built to produce panic in the reader.

sensory-pleasures.why: Incense, silks, moonlight, and music are described so the reader shares the court's pleasures.

aesthetic-pleasures.why: The hundreds of poems, the seasonal descriptions, and the prose itself are built as aesthetic experience; the tale is as much anthology as story.

piquancy.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

fun-excitement.why: The picture contest and festivals offer mild diversion; excitement is not the tale's aim.

orgasm.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

love-romantic.why: Genji's courtships and Kaoru's hopeless love are built to make the reader feel love's pull and cost.

love-family.why: The Kiritsubo Emperor's grief for Genji's mother and Genji raising little Murasaki are built to touch parental feeling.

grief.why: Murasaki's death and Genji's year of mourning, and the chapter title that is all that marks his own death, are built to make the reader grieve.

missing-someone.why: Longing is the tale's mood: the reader is made to feel every absence, from Genji's lost mother to Suma's exile to Kaoru outside Ukifune's door.

aroused-sexually.why: The liaisons are veiled behind curtains and poems; the reader is drawn, not aroused.

liking-as-a-friend.why: The reader is built to like Murasaki, Genji himself despite everything, and the loyal Koremitsu.

empathy.why: The narrator moves inside one woman after another, so the reader feels Rokujō's humiliation, Murasaki's hurt, and Ukifune's dilemma from within.

compassion.why: Suetsumuhana forgotten in her ruined house, Murasaki neglected, and Ukifune at the river are built to produce pity.

grateful.why: Nothing is built to make the reader feel gratitude.

pleasure-from-helping.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

trustful-distrustful.why: The reader knows of Reizei's parentage and Kaoru's before the characters do, and watches lies being told.

depressed.why: The Uji chapters' bleakness can lower the reader's mood, but the tale aims at melancholy rather than despair.

angry.why: Genji's treatment of the Third Princess and of Murasaki may anger a reader, but the narrator does not build anger.

envious.why: Nothing is built to produce envy.

jealous-romantic-sexual.why: Rokujō's and Murasaki's jealousy are rendered from inside so the reader feels their sting.

jealous-friendship.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

hatred.why: No character is built to be hated; even Kokiden is a political rival.

contempt.why: Suetsumuhana's old-fashioned verses invite a smile of condescension, nothing more.

resentment.why: The reader is made to feel the women's grievance at Genji's neglect and at the rules that bind them.

proud.why: Nothing is built to make the reader proud.

amused.why: Genji painting his nose red, the rainy-night ranking of women, and Suetsumuhana's gaucheries are built for gentle comedy.

sense-of-belonging.why: The reader is admitted to the inner life of the court but not recruited to a side.

lonely.why: Women waiting through the night and Genji at Suma are built to make the reader feel isolation.

judgy-moral-sense.why: The narrator invites judgment of Genji's affair with Fujitsubo and of Kashiwagi's, and of Genji's own eventual comeuppance.

admiration.why: The reader is told on every page of Genji's beauty, dancing, and verse, and meant to share the court's wonder.

embarrassed.why: Suetsumuhana's gift robe and Genji caught by Oborozukiyo's father produce secondhand embarrassment.

shame.why: The reader feels Kashiwagi's shame from within as he wastes away, but is not shamed.

guilt.why: Nothing is built to make the reader feel guilt.

sad.why: Mono no aware, the sadness of things, is the effect the whole tale is built to produce.

happy.why: The Rokujō years give the reader a brief contentment designed to be lost.

joyful-euphoric.why: Genji's recall from exile gives a lift the tale soon shadows.

effort.why: A thousand pages with characters named by shifting titles demand real persistence from a first-time reader.

focused-in-flow.why: The Uji chapters and the Suma exile can absorb a reader, but the tale's episodic drift does not aim at flow.

bored.why: Long stretches of ceremony and poem exchange test attention; the slowness is partly the design.

distracted.why: Nothing is built to distract the reader.

impatient.why: The reader may grow impatient with Kaoru's hesitations, which the tale draws out on purpose.

curious.why: The reader wants to know whether the secrets of Reizei and Kaoru will surface and what becomes of Ukifune.

surprised.why: Yūgao's sudden death and Ukifune's reappearance at Ono are built to startle; most turns are gradual.

awe.why: The Blue Sea Waves dance and the storm at Suma give the reader moments of wonder.

skeptical-doubtful.why: The narrator's occasional disclaimers invite a flicker of doubt about the telling, nothing more.

feeling-of-knowing.why: The reader recognizes Fujitsubo in Murasaki and Ōigimi in Ukifune before the characters say so, a designed sense of resemblance.

confused.why: Characters named only by shifting court titles leave a first-time reader often unsure who is who, a confusion the form produces.

frustrated.why: The tale ends with Kaoru turned from Ukifune's door and nothing resolved, a frustration built into the close.

uncertain-certain.why: The reader cannot be sure whether Ukifune will choose Kaoru or Niou, nor what the ending means.

understanding.why: The reader comes to understand Genji's story as karmic pattern when the Third Princess affair repeats Fujitsubo's.

inspired.why: Nothing is built to give the reader a flash of insight.

satisfied.why: The tale closes without closure, so the reader is left wanting rather than satisfied.

foreboding.why: The physiognomist's prophecy and the reader's foreknowledge of karmic return make every affair feel doomed.

nostalgia.why: The later chapters look back on the Shining Prince, and the reader is made to feel the loss of that world.

anticipation-suspense.why: The reader waits for secrets to break and for Ukifune's choice, but the tale is built for reverie more than suspense.

hope.why: The reader is allowed to hope for Murasaki's happiness and Ukifune's escape.

schadenfreude.why: Genji's fall from his own sin gives the reader a muted sense of justice.

elevation.why: Genji's care for Suetsumuhana and the Bishop's rescue of Ukifune offer small lifts.

infatuation.why: The reader is drawn into Genji's and Kashiwagi's obsessions by being placed inside them.

rage.why: Rokujō's possessing spirit gives the reader a shiver rather than rage.
